headline: Europe's Fire Salamanders Hide a Glowing Secret
meta_description: Scientists discover fire salamanders fluoresce green and cyan under UV light, a hidden ability that may help them communicate or warn predators of their toxins.
summary_short: Researchers at the Max Planck Institute have uncovered a surprising ability in Europe's black-and-yellow fire salamanders: they glow vivid green and cyan under ultraviol…
body:
Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Chemical Ecology have discovered that Europe's fire salamanders possess a hidden luminescence: under ultraviolet light, their distinctive yellow markings glow vivid green and cyan. The fluorescence originates primarily from glands in the salamanders' skin and their toxic secretions, which can remain fluorescent for more than 24 hours after being released. This biofluorescence—where organisms absorb UV light and reemit it as visible light—has remained undetected for decades despite fire salamanders being among Europe's most recognizable amphibians, known for their striking black-and-yellow coloring and chemical defenses. Bernat Burriel, lead researcher at the Museum of Natural Sciences in Barcelona, notes that the discovery "reminds us that even the most familiar organisms can hide secrets that are only revealed when they are observed with new tools."

While the phenomenon is confirmed, its biological purpose remains a mystery. Scientists propose two leading hypotheses: the glow may serve as communication, helping salamanders recognize each other in nocturnal or dense forest environments, or it may enhance their existing warning coloration to alert predators of their toxicity. Under full moonlight—which contains more ultraviolet and violet wavelengths than daylight—the green and cyan highlights against the salamanders' yellow markings could make individuals easier to spot. Remarkably, salamander skin chemistry has been studied for decades, making this discovery particularly surprising.

Perhaps most intriguing is that the chemical compound responsible for the fluorescence has not yet been identified, with evidence suggesting it may be a molecule previously unknown in the species. Identifying this compound could unlock deeper understanding of how these vulnerable amphibians, increasingly threatened by habitat destruction, interact with their forest ecosystems and communicate in the darkness.
quick_facts: Fire salamanders glow green and cyan under ultraviolet light
Fluorescent secretions remain glowing for over 24 hours
Discovered by Max Planck Institute researchers in 2026
Chemical compound behind glow remains unidentified
Could serve communication or predator-warning function
